Rome thought it was winning. Every step forward was carrying its soldiers deeper into a trap.
At Cannae, in two hundred and sixteen BC, Hannibal's center gave ground. Roman infantry surged into the narrowing space.
Now watch the sides. African infantry turned inward against Rome's flanks. Then Hannibal's cavalry, after winning its own fight, struck from behind.
More soldiers no longer meant more strength. Packed together, many could barely reach the fighting. The advance had become an enclosure.
But this wasn't effortless. Hannibal's center had to survive brutal pressure long enough for those other attacks to work.
Rome suffered a catastrophic defeat at Cannae. Yet Hannibal still lost the war. Winning this battle wasn't enough to break Rome.
